::: {.callout-note}
## In Layman's Terms

When a long train starts moving, the engine jerks forward first, then the first car, then the next, because each coupling has a little play that closes in turn. If you could only hear the clanks, you could still tell which end the engine is on. A golfer holds the club with two hands, and the motion of the club only tells you the total twist the hands put on it, not how much each hand gave. This page asks whether the order in which small gaps at the hands close could act like the train's clanks. It uses made-up computer models only. The short answer is that the clanks help only in tidy cases, and a hidden squeeze between the hands can fake them.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Status: Draft Under Review

This is a draft for the publication gate on [AffineDrift #5136](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/issues/5136). Every number below comes from manufactured models with declared parameters, generated by `python -m scripts.build_slack_takeup_witness` into `data/slack_takeup_witness/results.json`. The open blockers are scoped out, not resolved: there are no instrumented-grip data (UpstreamDrift VAR-03 to VAR-05 are deferred), the null-space record is "publication blocked", and the critique `nullspace_interpretation` is open with no adjudication evidence registered. This page therefore uses "identifiable" only in the narrow sense of the toy models defined here.
:::

## The Question {#sec-question}

A railway review defines slack action as "the progressive increase or decrease of inter-wagon distance being propagated through the train", and describes a start from a compressed train in which the locomotive moves, takes up the slack to the first wagon, and the momentum "would progress along the train" [@wagner2021draftgear]. The order of those take-up events is a record of where the pull came from.

A club held in two hands is different in one important way. Each hand applies a force and a couple (a pure twisting moment) to the club. The motion of the club fixes only their sum, the net wrench (force plus moment). Whatever part of the two hands' loads cancels on the club, such as the hands twisting against each other, cannot be seen in the club's motion. In the record, this cancelling set is the kernel of the grasp map $G$, the $6\times12$ matrix that turns the two hands' loads into the net wrench, and it has six dimensions (`UpstreamDrift:docs/research/loop_nullspace/loop_nullspace.tex` L524 at [`3fd2a59e`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/3fd2a59e390523169df846a3bbb395a6203c382c/docs/research/loop_nullspace/loop_nullspace.tex#L524)). Closed-chain inverse dynamics is therefore underdetermined, and "Regularization selects an allocation consistent with a penalty; it does not measure the selected internal forces" ([Inverse Dynamics](inverse-dynamics.html), L54 at [`20584d47`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/20584d47702c3b6f50a14728efc2fe2855561241/articles/inverse-dynamics.qmd#L54)).

The hypothesis under test, not a finding, is that small gaps or compliances at the hands, wrists and forearms engage in an order and with latencies that act as extra observations, and so shrink the set of allocations that fit the data. It restates the open High critique `nullspace_interpretation` ([critiques/adjudication-summary.md](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/20584d47702c3b6f50a14728efc2fe2855561241/critiques/adjudication-summary.md#L36) L36) as a computation.

This page covers identifiability only. The firm-lead-wrist and preload reading of slack, and its link to the heavy hit, belongs to [#5134](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/issues/5134). The choice of slack representation and the strategies for managing slack belong to [#5135](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/issues/5135). Neither is repeated here.

## The Counting Argument {#sec-counting}

Write the unknowns of an instant as a vector $x$ and the balance equations as $Ax=b$. Let $N$ be a matrix whose columns span the null space of $A$, the directions that change $x$ without changing $b$. If extra measurements $y=E_x x$ are taken, the record's count is
$$
\text{nullity after observation}=\operatorname{nullity}(A)-\operatorname{rank}(E_xN).
$$ {#eq-nullity}
Slack changes this count in two opposite ways. Each slack element adds unknowns: a half-gap $\delta$ (half the width of the dead band), a stiffness $k$, a damping and a starting state, meaning where in its band the element sits at $t=0$, or how far beyond the edge it is already pressed. If its take-up time can be observed, it also adds one observation. Stack the original null coordinates and the new slack parameters into an augmented vector $p$. Let $t_{\mathrm{ev}}$ be the vector of event times, and let $J=\partial t_{\mathrm{ev}}/\partial p$ be its Jacobian (the matrix of first derivatives). To first order, a quantity such as the torque split is determined by the events exactly when its direction lies in the row space of $J$. This is the invariance test of [After One Solution](after-one-solution-null-space-exploration.html#prop-p4), applied to event times instead of balance rows. With finite timing resolution, the record's test scales $J$ by the timing uncertainty $\sigma_t$, and a scaled singular value below one counts as unresolved. The train analogy works only if the event times respond to the source and not to the slack parameters. This page computes that; it does not assume it.

## Toy A: The Train, as a Positive Control {#sec-toy-a}

Four equal cars move along one line, joined by three couplers. Each coupler transmits no force while its stretch $e$ (the change in spacing between the two cars it joins) stays inside the band $|e|<\delta$, and acts as a spring with damping once $|e|\ge\delta$. A constant drive is applied either to the front car or to the rear car. Gaps and stiffnesses vary by $\pm50\%$ between trials, and each coupler starts at a random point covering 80% of its band. The fixed rule "the end whose coupler takes up first is the driven end" is right in 100.0% of 400 trials.

![Coupler Stretch of a Nominal Four-Car Train Driven at the Front (Left) and at the Rear (Right). Dashed Lines Are the Band Edges and Dotted Lines the Take-Up Times.](figures/slack_takeup_witness/train-takeup-order.svg){#fig-train fig-alt="Two panels of coupler stretch against time. With front drive, couplers one, two and three reach the upper band edge in that order; with rear drive, couplers three, two and one reach the lower edge in that order."}

The rule cannot fail here because each car stays at rest until the coupler ahead of it engages, so the first event must be next to the driven car. Start the train taut, with every coupler already at its tension edge, and the front-drive trials produce no take-up at all. The rule then falls to 74.2%: it is right whenever the train is pushed from the rear and right only by chance when it is pulled. A taut start makes the witness go silent, which echoes the preload limit in @tbl-record.

## Toy B: Two Hands Driving One Club {#sec-toy-b}

Toy B keeps one rotation axis. A lead hand (rotational inertia $0.01\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$), a club ($0.05\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$) and a trail hand ($0.01\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$) sit in a line, and each hand connects to the club through a dead-zone coupler with half-gap $0.012$ rad and stiffness $600$ N m/rad, the magnitudes of the record's synthetic dead-zone definition. A total drive of $10$ N m is split so that the lead hand receives a fraction $\alpha$ (the split) and the trail hand $1-\alpha$. A lead-source trial has $\alpha\in[0.6,0.8]$ and a trail-source trial has $\alpha\in[0.2,0.4]$. The witness is the pair of take-up times of the two couplers, each with $0.5$ ms of declared timing noise. A lag threshold is fitted on 400 training trials and scored on 400 held-out trials. The pass rule was fixed in the code before the first run: the lower end of the held-out 95% Wilson interval must exceed chance (50%) by 20 percentage points.

| Regime | Nuisance | Held-out accuracy | Wilson 95% interval | Pass |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Known slack | gaps, states and stiffness fixed | 100.0% | 99.0% to 100.0% | yes |
| Uncertain slack | gaps and stiffness $\pm50\%$, states over 80% of the band | 80.2% | 76.1% to 83.9% | yes |
| Preloaded | as above, plus an internal squeeze of 0 to 5 N m | 65.0% | 60.2% to 69.5% | no |
| Smooth spring | no gap at all | 52.8% | 47.9% to 57.6% | no |

: Held-out classification of the source hand in Toy B. {#tbl-toy-b}

The binary label survives bounded uncertainty in this toy, but the split itself does not. @fig-sensitivity shows the scaled Jacobian: each entry is the shift in a take-up time when one parameter moves by its declared prior half-range, in units of timing noise. The lead take-up time responds to the split, the lead gap and the lead starting state with comparable strength, and the trail time likewise. Two observations cannot separate seven unknowns. The split column has norm 7.39, so it would be resolved if every nuisance parameter were known. With the nuisance parameters free, the split direction has a component of 0.72 outside the row space of $J$, so it is not a first-order identifiable quantity. In the preloaded regime, 31.5% of held-out trials have no take-up event at all, and the smooth-spring regime has none by construction: a smooth law has no instant of take-up to observe.

![Scaled Event-Time Sensitivities in Toy B at a Lead Share of 0.6: Shift per Prior Half-Range in Units of the 0.5 ms Timing Noise.](figures/slack_takeup_witness/event-time-sensitivity.svg){#fig-sensitivity fig-alt="A two-row heat map. The lead take-up row has similar-sized entries for split, lead gap and lead state; the trail take-up row has similar-sized entries for split, trail gap and trail state; stiffness entries are near zero."}

A direct counterexample makes the point. A lead-led trial with $\alpha=0.7$ and centred slack takes up at 5.85 ms and 9.38 ms. A trail-led trial with $\alpha=0.3$, a trail gap at the top of its prior range and slack states inside the prior, takes up at 5.84 ms and 8.94 ms. The worst mismatch, 0.44 ms, is below the declared timing noise, and the club angles of the two trials never differ by more than 0.0016 rad (@fig-pair). The search stopped at the edge of the declared prior, so a wider prior would close the remaining gap.

![Coupler Stretch (Left) and Club Angle (Right) for a Lead-Led Trial and a Trail-Led Trial Whose Take-Up Times Agree Within Timing Noise.](figures/slack_takeup_witness/matched-pair.svg){#fig-pair fig-alt="Left, four stretch curves for the two trials with dotted take-up times nearly coinciding. Right, two club-angle curves that lie on top of each other over 60 milliseconds."}

## An Independent Check: First-Order Take-Up {#sec-first-order}

Argon's independent verification in [AffineDrift #5140](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/pull/5140) (`docs/development/technical-review/proposal-5136-slack-takeup-train-verification.md` at [`41812816`](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/41812816241939850937dc99b47a2aac5ec2da2e/docs/development/technical-review/proposal-5136-slack-takeup-train-verification.md)) uses a different representation, and this page reproduces it in `src/tools/slack_takeup_first_order.py`. Each hand channel relaxes toward its band edge with the record's 18 ms torque-development time $T$. Write the hand torques as $\tau_{\mathrm{lead}}=5-s$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{trail}}=5+s$ N m, so the internal torque $s$ is the null-space coordinate and $s>0$ means the trail hand supplies more. A channel with remaining gap $d=\delta-x(0)$, where $x(0)$ is its starting deflection, engages at
$$
t=T\ln\!\Bigl(1+\frac{k\,d}{\tau}\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-first-order}
Each time depends on $s$ and on its own remaining gap, so the $2\times3$ Jacobian in $(s,d_{\mathrm{lead}},d_{\mathrm{trail}})$ has rank 2, with one exact unobservable direction. At $s=0$ and $d=\delta$, each time moves by 2.125 ms per N m of $s$ and by 0.885 ms per mrad of gap. A 1 N m change in $s$ is therefore cancelled exactly by a 2.4 mrad change in each remaining gap, in opposite directions for the two hands.

Marginalizing the gaps under an 8 mrad prior, with a 2.5 N m prior on $s$, gives a scaled singular value of 0.866 at a timing resolution of 5 ms: below one, so the split is not resolved. The 5 ms value borrows the record's censoring horizon as a conservative resolution and is not a measured sensor property. At the 0.5 ms jitter used in Toy B the value is 1.058, barely above one. The gap prior, not the clock, limits what the events can say.

Flipping the preload gives an exact counterexample. With zero preload and $s=+2$ N m (trail-led), the channels engage at 22.03 ms and 12.73 ms, trail first. With $s=-2$ N m (lead-led) and starting deflections of -16.000 mrad (lead, pressed beyond the far edge of its 12 mrad band) and 6.857 mrad (trail), the engagement times are identical to machine precision. The event pattern says "trail" while the lead hand is the source.

## Toy C: Which Internal Directions Could Slack See? {#sec-toy-c}

Toy C uses the record's spatial grasp map with the hands 0.06 m either side of the club reference point along the shaft. The six internal coordinates are half the difference of the two hands' forces (axial squeeze along the shaft and two transverse shears) and half the difference of their couples (a twist couple about the shaft and two bending couples). Treat a slack channel at its most informative, as if it measured its wrench component continuously, and count the rank of that measurement on the kernel basis $K$ [@murray1994mathematical]. This is an upper bound: a real take-up event gives one time per engagement, not a continuous signal.

| Slack channel | Rank on the kernel | Hidden internal directions |
|---|---|---|
| None | 0 | all six |
| Force axes, both hands | 3 | twist and both bending couples |
| Couple (wrist rotation) axes, both hands | 5 | axial squeeze |
| Twist axis only | 1 | all but the twist couple |
| Every axis except axial force | 5 | axial squeeze |
| Every axis | 6 | none |

: Exact ranks of idealized slack channels on the six-dimensional grasp kernel. {#tbl-toy-c}

The proposal expected wrist rotational slack to see the twist and bending couples only, which would be rank 3. That expectation was wrong, as Argon's check found: the rank is 5. Through the lever arm between the hands, the couples also carry the two transverse shear forces. Their column norm is 0.0849, against 1.4142 for the couples, so they are seen about 16.7 times more weakly at this hand spacing. Axial squeeze has column norm exactly zero, because a force along the shaft has no lever arm about the shaft. Each hand's couple is $c=\mp d\times f_{\mathrm{diff}}\mp c_{\mathrm{diff}}$, and $d\times f$ vanishes for $f$ along $d$. @fig-nullity collects the counts.

![Unresolved Dimensions After Observation in Toy B and the First-Order Representation (Blue) and for the Toy C Slack Channels (Orange).](figures/slack_takeup_witness/nullity-counts.svg){#fig-nullity fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of nullity: rigid grip 1, slack with known nuisance 0, slack with free nuisance 5, first-order take-up 1, and Toy C channels 6, 3, 1, 5, 1 and 0."}

## Where the Train Analogy Breaks {#sec-breaks}

1. **Dimension.** A coupler acts along one line. The grip has six internal directions, and @tbl-toy-c shows that no single channel sees all of them.
2. **Gap versus smooth compliance.** A coupler has free slack. Tissue may be mostly smooth and stiffening, and a smooth law has no take-up instant (@tbl-toy-b, last row). Whether human grip slack has discrete gaps is open.
3. **Memory and direction.** Real draft gear has "a hysteresis loop due to the different behaviour in loading and unloading" [@bosso2020longtrain], and backlash keeps memory ([Sources of Nonlinearity](sources-of-nonlinearity.html#backlash-mechanical-play)). The dead zones here are memoryless, so history effects are untested.
4. **Two drivers.** The train has one engine. Two hands can push against each other with zero net load, so take-up can reflect the internal squeeze rather than its source (@sec-first-order).
5. **Active elements.** Couplers are passive. Muscles change stiffness and preload within a swing, so the "slack" is itself controlled. That is not modelled here.
6. **Bandwidth.** The take-up times here lie between 5.84 ms and 22.03 ms. The record's natural events are right-censored at 5 ms, and impact contact is shorter than any neural correction ([Heavy Hit and Impact Coupling](technology-heavy-hit-impact-coupling.html#sec-impact-timescales)).

## What Would Falsify the Idea, and What to Measure {#sec-falsifiers}

The idea fails if any of the following holds on real data: event timing becomes insensitive to the source hand once gap and preload uncertainty are marginalized; smooth-compliance models fit as well as gap models; impulses applied at a known hand do not produce the predicted take-up order; or preload changes alone reproduce the observed order. The synthetic results already show the last failure is possible in principle (@sec-first-order).

Measurement is worth planning only for the regimes that passed here. The plan would combine a high-rate bilateral six-axis grip wrench with pressure arrays, which is the only direct check on the internal wrench and the binding blocker (VAR-03 at L279 of `publication_gate.md`). It would add accelerometers on forearms, hands and shaft to time engagement onsets, EMG for timing only, and known-location impulses as ground truth. Because the gap prior dominates (@sec-first-order), any such study must calibrate each subject's slack state before the event, or the events cannot speak to the source. Engineering methods for identifying and compensating backlash and dead zones [@nordin2002backlash; @tao1994deadzone], and observability tests for hybrid systems [@bemporad2000observability; @vidal2003hybrid; @kong2024saltation], are context for that design. Whether their specific results transfer to tissue is TODO(source), pending research-scout.

## Claim Status {#sec-status}

- **Established (mathematics of the declared models):** the rank counts in @tbl-toy-c and @sec-first-order, the null direction, and the exact preload flip.
- **Modeled (synthetic, declared parameters):** the classification rates in @tbl-toy-b, the sensitivity map and the matched pair. They are not golfer results.
- **Open:** whether real grip, wrist or forearm slack has discrete gaps and of what size; whether take-up order differs between golfers or strategies; whether any slack observation reduces the closed-loop null space for real data.
- **TODO(source):** further train-dynamics references proposed in review (Garg and Dukkipati 1984; Cole 2006) have not been checked against their text, and the hybrid-observability and backlash sources are cited for their titles only.
